director.chapterArc: The chapter begins as an apparent interception, then reverses into a deliberately courteous recruitment interview. Callie and Katori test one another through tactical knowledge, disclosure, and silence; the Ember reveal changes the scale of the encounter without changing its businesslike tone. Callie then turns employment into protection for her mother, and Katori’s immediate acceptance establishes trust without sentimentality. Dry road humor releases the tension before the closing exchange turns toward Callie’s unnamed coming-of-age fear and the promise that she will not face it without somewhere to belong.
director.restraintNote: Keep Original Calder measured and observant. Let competence, withheld breath, and exact terms carry the tension. The Ember is a physical tool, not spectacle; care remains practical; grief is stated flatly; humor stays dry and unadvertised. Restore the base narrator immediately after every colored passage.

cues.delivery: Let Pell’s one-note amusement land like a dry mechanical click; he values the first civil exchange more as data than fellowship.
cues.from: Pell laughed — a dry, one-note thing, like a latch. He was sixty-odd, grey to the ears, sitting on an upturned crate with a book open on his knee and a pencil stub going behind it. "There it is," he said. "First civil word out of anybody this morning. Katori, take a note."
cues.through: Pell laughed — a dry, one-note thing, like a latch. He was sixty-odd, grey to the ears, sitting on an upturned crate with a book open on his knee and a pencil stub going behind it. "There it is," he said. "First civil word out of anybody this morning. Katori, take a note."
cues.reason: Pell’s dry wit provides the first controlled release from the standoff.

cues.delivery: Register Callie’s contained perceptual shock while describing every object and movement literally; the wonder lies in the impossible absence of ceremony.
cues.from: There was a blade in her hand.
cues.through: Then her hand was empty again. There was a flat grey slab in it, about the size of her palm, three fingers thick, rounded at the corners. She turned it over once and put it in her coat.
cues.reason: The mundane manifestation of the Ember decisively changes Callie’s understanding of Katori.

cues.delivery: Make the demand hard, contractual, and protective; Callie is testing whether her mother will be treated as a burden, not pleading for kindness.
cues.from: "Not the whole wagon. That third." Callie pointed. "My mother rides. Not when it's bad. Every day, all day, whether it's bad or not, and nobody gets to have a face about it on the days it isn't."
cues.through: "Not the whole wagon. That third." Callie pointed. "My mother rides. Not when it's bad. Every day, all day, whether it's bad or not, and nobody gets to have a face about it on the days it isn't."
cues.reason: Callie converts the negotiation into an uncompromising act of protection.

cues.delivery: Hold the line without raising pressure; the effort is in refusing to turn and refusing to let her mother diminish the term.
cues.from: "You're not," Callie said, and did not turn around, and kept her eyes on Katori, and found it took everything she had.
cues.through: "You're not," Callie said, and did not turn around, and kept her eyes on Katori, and found it took everything she had.
cues.reason: Callie’s restraint nearly breaks under the cost of asserting her mother’s need.

cues.delivery: Give Pell’s warning the exactness of bookkeeping and only the faintest human concern; he offers Callie honesty, not reassurance.
cues.from: "It's noted." He looked up at her over the top of the atlas. He had the pale, water-coloured eyes that very old men on the road sometimes had, and he was not unkind, and he was also not going to pretend at anything. "I've been keeping this book eleven years and it'll tell you every mile and every ounce and what we paid for it. The one thing it doesn't have a column for is what a thing's worth. You'll want to work that out for yourself before the gate. Meridian has columns."
cues.through: "It's noted." He looked up at her over the top of the atlas. He had the pale, water-coloured eyes that very old men on the road sometimes had, and he was not unkind, and he was also not going to pretend at anything. "I've been keeping this book eleven years and it'll tell you every mile and every ounce and what we paid for it. The one thing it doesn't have a column for is what a thing's worth. You'll want to work that out for yourself before the gate. Meridian has columns."
cues.reason: Pell quietly prepares Callie for Meridian’s colder valuation of people.

cues.delivery: Let Otto attempt the joke with complete earnestness, then allow the embarrassment to catch him only after it has escaped.
cues.from: "That's the corner of the world," said Otto, very seriously, "digging in," and then went red, and went to see to the team.
cues.through: "That's the corner of the world," said Otto, very seriously, "digging in," and then went red, and went to see to the team.
cues.reason: Otto’s accidental wit releases pressure while defining his careful temperament.

cues.delivery: Deliver the horse analysis as sober risk specification; never signal the joke, especially on the final measurement.
cues.from: "She's a horse." Pell said it the way another man would have said a number. "That's not an insult, it's a specification. A mule will look at a bad thing and stop and stand there and refuse you all afternoon, and you can hit it and it'll go on refusing you, and that refusing has saved my life twice. A horse looks at a bad thing and leaves. That's all a horse is. It's four hundred kilos of leaving, and the only question is what's standing where it decides to leave through."
cues.through: "She's a horse." Pell said it the way another man would have said a number. "That's not an insult, it's a specification. A mule will look at a bad thing and stop and stand there and refuse you all afternoon, and you can hit it and it'll go on refusing you, and that refusing has saved my life twice. A horse looks at a bad thing and leaves. That's all a horse is. It's four hundred kilos of leaving, and the only question is what's standing where it decides to leave through."
cues.reason: Pell’s factual cadence turns danger assessment into character-defining dry comedy.

cues.delivery: Land the contradiction with ledger-flat certainty; affection and prudence occupy separate categories for Pell.
cues.from: "I like her enormously," Pell said. "That's a separate column."
cues.through: "I like her enormously," Pell said. "That's a separate column."
cues.reason: The separate-column line completes the comic argument without softening Pell.

cues.delivery: State the absence plainly, with no bid for sympathy; the loss is old enough to function as a fact and deep enough to need no ornament.
cues.from: "There wasn't anybody left in my town to do the words over anybody."
cues.through: "There wasn't anybody left in my town to do the words over anybody."
cues.reason: Callie’s answer exposes the human cost beneath her unnamed anxiety.

cues.delivery: Keep Katori practical and absolute: she dismisses the ritual’s power while quietly offering the belonging that matters.
cues.from: "No," said Katori. "Not one bit. But it's better to have somewhere to be."
cues.through: "No," said Katori. "Not one bit. But it's better to have somewhere to be."
cues.reason: Katori answers Callie’s deeper fear without forcing her to name it.
